questions.explanation: The four UNESCO World Heritage Baroque churches (1993): (1) San Agustin Church, Manila — oldest surviving stone church (completed 1607); (2) San Agustin Church, Paoay — PRIMARY Earthquake Baroque with 14 massive buttresses; (3) Nuestra Señora de la Asunción, Santa Maria — hilltop fortress-like appearance; (4) Santo Tomás de Villanueva, Miagao — 'Fortress Baroque' with tropical facade showing St. Christopher with coconut palms and papaya.

Industrial buildings at the center and civic buildings hidden at the edge.
No plaza, no civic center, and no religious anchor.

questions.rationale: Main plaza at the center with the church, tribunal, government buildings, and marketplace around it. HOA Module 4 P1 describes the plaza complex around the main plaza.
questions.explanation: The San Agustin Church in Paoay, Ilocos Norte (UNESCO World Heritage, 1993) is the quintessential Earthquake Baroque structure. Its 14 massive buttresses are aligned linearly along the church's exterior walls. Unlike decorative European buttresses, these are load-bearing seismic elements: their angled orientation converts lateral earthquake forces into compressive forces directed into the ground, preventing the thick walls from toppling. The Paoay Church also has a coral-stone bell tower detached from the main structure — another seismic isolation measure.

questions.explanation: SCMTE: Simbahan (Church — dominant position, tallest structure, bell tower as landmark), Convento (adjacent parish house), Municipio (government seat), Tribunal (court/administrative), Escuela (near church/convento). Memory hook: 'Sa Church May Tribunal at Eskwela.' The plaza complex physically expressed centralized colonial authority — the church anchored religious power, the municipio anchored civil authority, the marketplace anchored economic life. Streets radiated from the plaza in a gridiron (quadícula) pattern, with eight streets exiting from the four corners.

questions.rationale: Main plaza at the center with the church, tribunal, government buildings, and marketplace around it. HOA Module 4 P1 describes the plaza complex around the main plaza.
questions.explanation: The Laws of the Indies specified that remaining lots were distributed by lottery to settlers, with lots closer to the plaza assigned first. Elite residences (bahay na bato) were on lots closest to the plaza, expressing the social hierarchy spatially — proximity to the plaza meant proximity to political and religious power. Common residences progressively farther from the plaza housed ordinary townspeople on blocks radiating outward.

questions.rationale: An elevated location, orderly street grid, central plaza, defensive wall, and zones for church, commerce, government, hospitals, and slaughterhouses. HOA Module 4 P1 lists these Laws of the Indies characteristics.
questions.explanation: Ordinance 126 of the Laws of the Indies explicitly states 'In the plaza, no lots shall be assigned to private individuals.' This provision physically enforced the plaza as a civic rather than commercial/private space. In practice, however, elite residences (bahay na bato) were assigned on lots closest to the plaza — the proximity to power principle. The church was also sometimes built directly on the plaza in Philippine practice despite the ordinance calling for a slight separation with its own forecourt.

questions.rationale: The consolidation of formerly scattered barangays into larger compact communities for religious conversion and cultural change. HOA Module 4 P1 describes reduccion as compact resettlement of scattered barangays.
questions.explanation: Vigan is the best-preserved Spanish colonial town in Asia and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage City in 1999 precisely because it retains the Laws of the Indies urban structure: a central plaza surrounded by the cathedral, seminary, and municipal building, with streets radiating outward in a gridiron (quadricula) pattern. Calle Crisologo runs parallel to the plaza and exemplifies the arcade (portales) requirement of the Laws — arcaded walkways providing shade and shelter. The Laws also specified portales along the four principal streets — a tropical adaptation that 'provided considerable convenience to the merchants who generally gathered there.'

questions.rationale: A grid pattern of streets and blocks laid out with uniform precision. The checked source defines cuadricula as a grid of streets and blocks.
questions.explanation: The Laws of the Indies included portales (arcaded walkways) as a specific tropical adaptation — the Spanish crown recognized that colonial urban planning in Southeast Asia required protection from sun and rain. The ordinance's own language stated the portales were 'of considerable convenience to the merchants who generally gathered there.' Streets had to open onto the plaza 'without encountering these porticoes' — meaning the porticoes were set back to maintain clear sidewalks. This is a key detail that distinguishes Laws of the Indies urbanism in Asia from its American applications.
